name: Sabarimala Sri Dharma Sastha Temple (Ayyappan)
deity: Lord Ayyappan, worshipped as Dharma Sastha, seated in a yogic posture as a Naishtika Brahmachari, an eternal celibate. He is revered as Hariharaputra, held to be the son of Shiva and of Mohini, a form of Vishnu.
tradition: Ayyappa or Dharma Sastha worship, a synthesis of Shaiva and Vaishnava devotion
period: Ancient origins; present sanctum rebuilt in 1950
dynasty: Traditions associate the temple with the Pandalam royal house
summary: Sabarimala is among the most visited pilgrimage centres in the world, drawing devotees who complete a demanding preparatory discipline before their journey. The shrine of Lord Ayyappan sits atop a forested hill in the Western Ghats of Pathanamthitta district, Kerala. It opens only during specific pilgrimage seasons rather than year round.

sections.history: The origins of worship at Sabarimala are held to be ancient, woven into the traditions of the Pandalam royal house and the forested Sastha shrines of the region. For centuries the hill drew devotees who trekked through dense forest to reach the deity. The present sanctum was rebuilt after a fire damaged the earlier structure in 1950, and later works added facilities for the very large numbers who now arrive each season. Through these changes the temple has kept its character as a forest shrine reached only on foot, and its disciplines of preparation and pilgrimage have been carried forward with care, linking present devotees to generations who made the same ascent before them.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Kerala idiom and is modest in scale for so celebrated a pilgrimage centre. The sanctum stands within a walled compound at Sannidhanam, the summit precinct, approached through the eighteen sacred steps known as the Pathinettam Padi. Only those who have kept the preparatory discipline and carry the irumudi offering bundle may climb these steps. Surrounding structures serve the flow of devotees, shelter the sacred fire and hold subsidiary shrines. Built and rebuilt with restraint, the complex sits within the forest of the Periyar Tiger Reserve, so that its setting of hill and tree is as much a part of the experience as the masonry itself.
sections.legends: Ayyappan is revered as Hariharaputra, born of Shiva and of Mohini, an enchanting form assumed by Vishnu, and so uniting the two great streams of devotion. In the tradition of the Pandalam house he is remembered as a princely child of miraculous origin, raised in the palace before returning to the forest to take his seat upon the hill. He is worshipped as a Naishtika Brahmachari, an eternal celibate seated in yogic stillness. The name Sabarimala is linked in tradition to Sabari, the devoted ascetic of the forest remembered in the epics. These accounts, told in many local forms, frame the deity as a protector of the forest and a guide to those who seek him with discipline.
sections.festivals: The temple opens chiefly for the Mandala and Makaravilakku season, running from about mid November to mid January, and for the first days of each Malayalam month. Makaravilakku, observed around Makara Sankranti in mid January, is the foremost occasion of the year, when great numbers gather and the appearance of the Makara Jyothi is central to the observance. The Mandala period frames the long weeks of the main pilgrimage. Because openings follow this calendar rather than a daily schedule, devotees plan their journey around the announced dates and should confirm the current schedule locally before travelling.
sections.experience: A pilgrimage to Sabarimala begins long before the hill, with a vratham of about forty one days in which devotees wear black or blue, set aside comforts, and address one another as Swami in a spirit of equality. Each carries the irumudi kettu, a two compartment bundle of offerings, upon the head, and the constant chant is Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa. Pilgrims reach the base at Pamba and then trek several kilometres uphill through forest to Sannidhanam. The final approach is by the eighteen sacred steps. The shared discipline, the forest path and the sound of the chant carried by thousands give the journey a quiet, absorbing intensity that many describe as its true reward.

visit.timings: The temple does not open year round. It opens chiefly for the Mandala and Makaravilakku pilgrimage season, roughly mid November to mid January, and for the first days of each Malayalam month, with darshan hours set within those openings. Because the schedule follows the Malayalam calendar and is announced season by season, verify the current schedule locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Pilgrims traditionally observe the vratham and wear black, blue or plain devotional clothing, and many keep the customary austerities before the ascent. Modest, simple dress is expected within the temple precinct.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted within the temple, especially around the sanctum and the sacred steps. Follow the posted rules and the directions of temple staff, and keep behaviour quiet and reverent.
visit.gettingThere: Pilgrims reach the base at Pamba by road, travelling via Pathanamthitta or Erumeli, then trek roughly four to five kilometres uphill through forest to the shrine at Sannidhanam. The nearest railheads are Chengannur and Kottayam, and the nearest airports are Kochi and Thiruvananthapuram.
